whatItIs.text: A Mediterranean mint-family herb, 'wild marjoram' to its relatives; its oil is up to 80% carvacrol and thymol, which is why the smell alone seasons a tomato sauce.

historyNote.text: The name may come from Greek for 'joy of the mountain' (orós + gános); garden-variety oregano is notably bland next to the Greek and Turkish species sold as the same herb, a fact that explains a lot of disappointing pizza.

howToChoose.text: For dried, choose deep green leaves with a pungent smell when crushed; for fresh, Greek-style oregano with firm leaves beats the soft garden type for cooking.

storage.text: Keep dried in an airtight tin away from light; fresh oregano keeps like other tender herbs. The rulebook has the guidance.

foodSafetyRef.note: herb storage windows live in the food-safety rulebook

useItUp.text: Crush dried oregano between your fingers into dressings, marinades, and slow tomato sauces.

substitutions.note: its sweet cousin; gentler, add later in cooking
